title: Event 1
content:
Summary Report: “Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam” Event information Item Details Event name Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam Speaker Dr. Werner Vogels, Chief Technology Officer of Amazon Date October 2, 2026 Location [ Bitexco Tower - Ho Chi Minh City] Role Attendee I attended this session to hear Dr. Werner Vogels talk about the future of software engineering. As a student who studies in class and also builds projects on my own, I often ask myself whether AI will replace programmers, so the topic felt very close to home. The whole hall kept taking notes, and each time the speaker mentioned AI the room grew noticeably quieter.
Key takeaways The outage on a peak shopping day. Mr. Vogels described Amazon’s early years: during the holiday shopping season the relational database was overwhelmed, the system went down for a full day and the company suffered heavy losses. What impressed me most was how the team responded. The software vendor argued that Amazon had used the product far beyond its design limits, and he openly agreed they were right. The engineers did not patch it up quickly. They stepped back and measured how the system was really used. The result showed that most queries were simple key-value lookups that did not need a heavy relational database. That finding gave rise to Dynamo and, later, DynamoDB. I use DynamoDB for the job and result-cache tables in the Trust Check project, so this story helped me understand why the service exists. Operational discipline. According to Mr. Vogels, looking at averages is an easy way to fool yourself, because an average hides the poor experience of users at both extremes. He stressed the mindset that “everything fails at some point”. Amazon runs drills on purpose, shutting down parts of its live infrastructure to see how well the system tolerates failure. The “Renaissance Developer”. This was my favorite part. Programmers will not be pushed out if they develop around five traits: curiosity, systems thinking, ownership, broad knowledge together with deep expertise, and communication skills. He compared AI to a natural-language compiler: very fast but able to make mistakes, so its output always needs a human to check it. Photos from the event Lessons learned and personal contribution AI writes the code, but the responsibility is mine. I used to take AI-generated code, run a quick test and put it straight into my project once it worked. After this session I set myself a rule: never commit a line of code I cannot explain. Before accepting code from AI, I will look at edge cases, security vulnerabilities and performance bottlenecks. Anything I do not understand, I cannot claim as my own work. Look at the whole system instead of isolated features. School assignments usually revolve around single modules. I will redraw the data flow of Trust Check from the interface, through API Gateway, SQS and Lambda, down to DynamoDB, and ask what happens if one component stops working. Major outages almost always start from assumptions that were never verified. Understand the real workload before choosing technology. I tend to pick tools simply because they are popular or talked about. Amazon’s story reminded me to start from how the system is actually used. From now on, before choosing a database or framework, I will list the kinds of queries and data processing the application really needs. The Trust Check cache table is looked up by a hash of the content, exactly the kind of key-value query Mr. Vogels described. Take communication skills seriously. I used to treat communication as a side matter. Now I see how it helps engineers find the real problem behind vague requests and explain technical trade-offs to non-technical people. I will practice writing concise documentation for my part of the work and presenting more often in group projects. Be wary of “we have always done it this way”. Mr. Vogels closed with Grace Hopper’s well-known warning about the most dangerous phrase in the language. For me it is a reminder to review and refresh, from time to time, how I learn and write code. I left the hall feeling more relieved than worried. What I took home was not an empty reassurance to “stop worrying about AI”, but a clearer view of what AI still cannot replace: judgment, systems thinking, accountability and professional pride. Those are the skills I need to build starting now. My first task this week is to redraw the architecture diagram of my current project and review all the code I previously let AI write for me.

title: Functional testing
content:
This section tests the three scanning flows of the system with harmless samples: a link, an email and a file. The web frontend started in section 5.4.9 is used for the main part. The last part tests the API directly.
Prepare the test samples The sample link and email are already in the source code (backend\samples). The two sample files must be created with PowerShell, in a folder of your choice:
mkdir workshop-samples cd workshop-samples Set-Content -Path ghi_chu.txt -Value "Bien ban hop nhom. Noi dung: ke hoach workshop." -Encoding ascii Set-Content -Path hoa_don_thang_11.pdf -Value "MZ This is an inert text file used only for testing the file scanner. It is not a program." -Encoding ascii ghi_chu.txt is plain text, used as a safe sample. hoa_don_thang_11.pdf is actually a harmless text file that begins with the characters MZ, the signature of a Windows executable. It simulates a file with a disguised extension. How to read a result Score Risk level 80 and above SAFE 50 to 79 SUSPICIOUS below 50 DANGEROUS A result also has confidence (HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW) showing how many external sources answered. A SAFE result with LOW confidence only means no bad signs were found and nothing was cross-checked with an external source. When the API keys from section 5.4.6 or 5.4.8 are configured, confidence is usually higher.
Test a link scan Open http://localhost:8000/index.html and choose the Link tab. Paste http://paypal-security-update-fake.com/login and submit. Wait for the result (a few seconds up to about a minute). Expected result: risk level DANGEROUS. Typical reasons: the domain contains the name “paypal” but is not the official site, it contains sensitive keywords (login, update, security), the domain has too many hyphens, and HTTPS is not used.
Control sample: scan https://example.com. The expected result is SAFE.
Test an email scan Open backend\samples\email_lua_dao.txt in Visual Studio Code, select all the content and copy it. In the web frontend, choose the Email tab, paste the content and submit. Expected result: risk level DANGEROUS. Typical reasons: the sender domain impersonates a brand, the display name impersonates another organisation, the email fails the DMARC policy, it contains pressure phrases, and the reply address differs from the sender domain.
Control sample: scan the content of backend\samples\email_binh_thuong.txt. The expected result is SAFE.
Test a file scan In the web frontend, choose the File tab. Select the file hoa_don_thang_11.pdf and submit. Expected result: risk level SUSPICIOUS, with the reason that the file has a .pdf extension but is actually an executable program.
Control sample: scan the file ghi_chu.txt. The expected result is SAFE.
Test directly through the API This part tests the asynchronous flow without the web frontend. Replace <INVOKE_URL> with the address recorded in section 5.4.7.
Scan a link and follow the status:
$base = "<INVOKE_URL>" $job = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan" -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body '{"type":"link","payload":"http://paypal-security-update-fake.com/login"}' $job do { Start-Sleep 5 $r = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan/$($job.job_id)" $r.status } while ($r.status -ne "COMPLETED") $r.result.risk_level $r.result.confidence $r.result.reasons The job status goes through PENDING, PROCESSING and then COMPLETED. Numeric values in the StatusLambda response can appear as strings (for example "45"), so convert them when using them in code.
Scan a file (two steps): the system returns an upload_url valid for 5 minutes. Upload the file to that address immediately, then ask for the result as usual.
$path = (Resolve-Path .\hoa_don_thang_11.pdf).Path $job = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan" -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body (@{type="file"; payload=(Split-Path $path -Leaf)} | ConvertTo-Json) Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $job.upload_url -Method Put -InFile $path -ContentType "application/octet-stream" do { Start-Sleep 5 $r = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan/$($job.job_id)" $r.status } while ($r.status -ne "COMPLETED") $r.result.risk_level Result Sample Expected risk level Link paypal-security-update-fake.com DANGEROUS Link example.com SAFE Email email_lua_dao.txt DANGEROUS Email email_binh_thuong.txt SAFE File hoa_don_thang_11.pdf SUSPICIOUS File ghi_chu.txt SAFE The exact score may differ depending on the data returned by the external sources. The risk level is the main criterion to compare.

title: Overview
content:
What Trust Check is Trust Check checks a link, an email or a file for signs of phishing or malware. Instead of a plain “safe” or “unsafe”, it gives you a trust score from 0 to 100 and tells you why points were deducted.
Score Level 80 – 100 SAFE 50 – 79 SUSPICIOUS below 50 DANGEROUS Each result also has a confidence field (HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW) showing how many reputable external sources answered. A SAFE score with LOW confidence only means no bad signs were found. It does not mean the content is confirmed safe.
What you will build API Gateway (HTTP API): receives POST /scan and GET /scan/{job_id}. Lambda (Python 3.12): four functions: IngestLambda, StatusLambda, FastDetectWorker, FileDetectWorker. SQS: phishing-fast-queue for links and emails, phishing-file-queue for files, and phishing-dlq for failed messages. DynamoDB: PhishingScanJobs for job state and results, PhishingScanCache for cached results with a TTL. S3: a bucket that receives files uploaded by users through presigned URLs. Systems Manager Parameter Store (optional): stores API keys as SecureString. CloudWatch: logs and metrics. A web frontend written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, running on your own machine. Outside AWS, the system also calls VirusTotal, Google Safe Browsing, URLhaus, MalwareBazaar and RDAP, all on free tiers.
By the end you will Understand what each service does and why links and emails are handled separately from files. Have deployed a complete serverless system in the AWS Console. Have tested it with sample links, emails and files, and read the score and reasons. Know where to look at logs, metrics and the dead-letter queue in CloudWatch and SQS. Have deleted every resource when you are done. General information Region: Singapore (ap-southeast-1). Time: about 2 to 3 hours (estimate). Cost: all services are pay-per-use and at workshop scale should mostly fit in the AWS Free Tier. Still check your Billing page and do section 5.6 when you finish. What is not included The workshop follows the current source code, so a few limits apply:
ClamAV only runs when the environment has clamscan. On regular Lambda it is skipped. YARA is a hand-written byte-string rule set, not the real YARA library. Email analysis uses English and Vietnamese rules, not a machine learning model. SPF, DKIM and DMARC are read from the email headers you paste in. The system does not query DNS itself. There is no PDF report export and no user login.

title: Prepare the source code
content:
Before creating any AWS resources, confirm that the source code runs correctly on the local machine and build the deployment package for the two worker functions.
Run the test suite Open PowerShell, change to the backend folder of the source code cloned in section 5.2, and run:
cd AWS-Phishing-Detection\backend python -m unittest discover -s tests -t . The test suite needs no network connection or AWS account. A successful run ends with the line Ran ... tests followed by OK.
The output may contain Traceback lines. These are logs from error cases that the tests trigger on purpose and are not real failures. The result is determined by the last line.
Build the deployment package In the backend folder, run:
python build_zip.py The command creates dist\detect-workers.zip (about 33 KB). The package contains the two handlers fast_detect_worker.py and file_detect_worker.py at the root of the zip, together with the common and detectors folders.
FastDetectWorker and FileDetectWorker share this package. IngestLambda and StatusLambda are each a single Python file, backend\ingest_lambda.py and backend\status_lambda.py, and need no packaging.
Result The test suite completes with status OK. The file backend\dist\detect-workers.zip has been created.

title: Blog 1
content:
AWS CONTINUUM: BRINGING PENETRATION TESTING INTO EVERY CI/CD DEPLOYMENT 1. Introduction In modern software development, applications are updated frequently. New features, configuration changes, and code modifications can introduce security weaknesses at any stage of the development lifecycle.
Traditional penetration testing is often performed periodically, such as before a major release or during a scheduled security assessment. Although valuable, this approach may leave changes made between testing cycles without immediate security validation.
At the same time, automated security tools such as SAST, DAST, and SCA help identify potential weaknesses, but their findings may still require further investigation to determine whether a vulnerability is actually exploitable.
AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing introduces a way to integrate penetration testing into CI/CD pipelines. It can automatically test an application after deployment to a pre-production environment and use the results as a security gate before production promotion.
AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing integrated into the CI/CD workflow. 2. Understanding the Key Concepts Before exploring the integration, it is important to understand several security and DevOps concepts.
2.1. SAST, DAST, and SCA SAST (Static Application Security Testing): Examines application source code or compiled code without executing the application to identify potential security weaknesses. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): Tests a running application by sending requests and observing its responses. SCA (Software Composition Analysis): Identifies third-party libraries and dependencies and checks them for known vulnerabilities or licensing issues. These tools provide useful security signals. However, their findings do not always demonstrate that a weakness can be exploited in the actual application environment.
2.2. Penetration Testing Penetration testing evaluates an application by simulating security attacks within an authorized scope. Its purpose is to determine whether weaknesses can be exploited and to understand their potential impact.
Unlike tools that primarily identify potential weaknesses, penetration testing can validate whether a security issue is practically exploitable.
2.3. CI/CD Pipeline CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery or Deployment. A pipeline automates stages such as building, testing, and deploying application changes.
A security gate can be inserted into this workflow so that a deployment must satisfy defined security requirements before proceeding to the next stage.
2.4. OpenID Connect (OIDC) OIDC allows a CI/CD provider to obtain temporary AWS credentials through identity federation. Instead of storing long-lived AWS access keys in pipeline variables, the workflow receives an OIDC token and exchanges it through AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) by assuming an IAM role.
3. Limitations of Traditional Security Testing Traditional security testing and automated scanning serve different purposes.
Automated tools help identify areas that may require attention, while penetration testing helps validate whether relevant weaknesses are exploitable.
When penetration testing is performed only at scheduled intervals, changes introduced after an assessment may remain untested until the next cycle. Performing a full penetration test for every deployment, on the other hand, may increase testing time and operational costs.
The challenge is therefore to make security testing continuous without unnecessarily testing the entire application after every small change.
4. How AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing Works AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing addresses this challenge by integrating a scoped penetration test into the deployment pipeline.
The general workflow is:
Developers commit application changes. The CI/CD pipeline builds and tests the application. The application is deployed to a staging or pre-production environment. The pipeline authenticates to AWS using OIDC. The integration starts a penetration test against the configured application and scope. AWS Continuum evaluates the test result and returns the outcome to the pipeline. The pipeline either allows or blocks promotion to production according to the configured rules. The penetration testing job runs on the AWS side. The CI/CD runner coordinates the integration and receives the result rather than executing the penetration testing logic itself.
4.1. Security Gate The security gate determines whether a deployment can proceed.
For example, if the configured severity threshold is HIGH, findings classified as HIGH or CRITICAL block promotion. Findings below the threshold are reported but do not block the pipeline.
This behavior is configurable. Teams can choose a threshold that matches their security requirements.
4.2. Understanding the Pipeline Result A failed pipeline does not necessarily mean that a confirmed vulnerability was found. The outcome must be interpreted using the test result and scope decision.
Important outcomes include:
Finding at or above the configured threshold: The gate fails and blocks promotion. Scoped out: The change is within the configured scope, but no security-relevant attack-surface change requires testing. The pipeline passes. Scope conflict: The change falls outside the configured penetration-testing scope. The pipeline follows the configured conflict-handling behavior. Infrastructure error: The test could not start or complete. Whether this blocks the pipeline depends on the fail-on-infrastructure-error setting. 5. Change-Based Scoping One of the important features of this integration is its ability to scope testing to application changes.
Instead of testing the entire application after every deployment, AWS Continuum determines the commit range between:
Head commit: The commit currently being evaluated. Base commit: The previous commit that the gate has already cleared. The integration uses this range to determine which changes need security testing.
Three scope decisions are particularly important:
Scope decision Meaning In scope The change modifies the tested attack surface and is evaluated by the penetration test. Scoped out The change does not modify the relevant attack surface, so the pipeline can pass without a new test. Scope conflict The change falls outside the configured test scope and was not tested. This approach helps reduce unnecessary testing while maintaining a clear record of which changes have been assessed.
6. Integrating AWS Continuum into CI/CD The integration generally involves three preparation steps.
6.1. Configure the Penetration Test First, configure the target application and its testing scope in AWS Continuum.
The target domain must be verified, and the penetration test must be configured with the appropriate target, credentials, and network scope.
CI/CD mode must then be enabled, and the required Agent Space ID and penetration test ID must be recorded.
The pipeline uses this existing configuration when starting a test. It does not create the target or penetration test automatically.
6.2. Configure IAM and OIDC Authentication Next, configure an IAM OIDC identity provider and an IAM role that the CI/CD workflow can assume.
The role requires two important policies:
Trust policy: Defines which CI/CD identities are allowed to assume the role. Permissions policy: Defines what the workflow can do after assuming the role. The trust policy should be restricted to the intended repository, branch, or deployment environment wherever supported.
Using OIDC and temporary credentials avoids the need to store long-lived AWS access keys in CI/CD variables.
6.3. Add the Security Gate to the Pipeline Finally, add the AWS Continuum penetration-testing step after the staging deployment.
The production deployment should depend on the successful completion of this security gate.
For example, in GitHub Actions, the production deployment job can declare the security-testing job as a dependency using needs.
This ensures that production promotion is skipped when the security gate fails.
7. Rolling Out the Gate: Report-only and Block Modes Enforcing a security gate immediately may interrupt existing development workflows. A gradual rollout can help teams understand the results before introducing blocking behavior.
7.1. Report-only Mode In report-only mode, the penetration test still runs and findings are collected and published, but the severity threshold is set to NONE so findings do not block the pipeline.
This allows teams to observe results and understand how the integration behaves before enforcing a threshold.
7.2. Block Mode After reviewing the results, teams can configure a threshold such as HIGH.
Findings at or above the selected threshold then cause the gate to fail and prevent production promotion.
However, three settings must be considered independently:
severity-threshold: Determines which findings block the pipeline. on-scope-conflict: Determines what happens when a change is outside the configured scope. fail-on-infrastructure-error: Determines whether infrastructure errors block the pipeline. 7.3. Important Baseline Consideration A successful report-only run can advance the commit baseline. This means that when the threshold is later changed to HIGH, previously cleared commits are not automatically tested again.
If an earlier commit range needs to be reassessed, the relevant base and head commit SHAs can be specified explicitly according to the integration documentation.
Teams should understand this behavior before moving from report-only to blocking mode.
8. Practical Security Considerations Several considerations are important when implementing this integration:
Start with a controlled rollout: Observe report-only results before enforcing blocking thresholds. Use OIDC: Prefer temporary credentials over long-lived access keys. Apply least privilege: Restrict the IAM role’s trust and permissions policies. Review scope conflicts: A change that was not tested should not be treated as equivalent to a successful penetration test. Handle infrastructure errors deliberately: If production promotion requires security sign-off, configure the gate to fail when the test cannot run. Protect pipeline configuration: Restrict who can modify workflow files and security-gate settings. Pin integration versions: Use an immutable release tag or commit SHA where supported, so upstream changes do not silently alter the pipeline integration. 9. Conclusion AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing provides a practical approach to integrating penetration testing into modern CI/CD workflows.
By testing changes after deployment, using commit-based scoping, and applying configurable security gates, teams can make security validation part of the release process rather than relying exclusively on periodic assessments.
The integration does not replace every security activity. Instead, it complements automated scanning, secure development practices, and broader security assessments by providing an additional validation stage before production deployment.
References AWS Security Blog – Penetration Testing Every Deployment with AWS Continuum AWS Documentation – Run Penetration Tests from Your CI/CD Pipeline AWS Documentation – GitHub Actions Integration Tutorial

Summary Report: “Buildrathon Kickoff: Code the Future with CMC Global” Event information Item Details Event name Buildrathon Kickoff: Code the Future with CMC Global Organizers AWS Study Group (First Cloud AI Journey), together with CMC Global Speakers Thien Lu (Program Manager, FCAJ), Truong Bui (Tech Lead, CMC Global), Phong Pham (Program Manager, FCAJ) Date and time 09:00 to 12:00, Saturday, September 26, 2026 Location 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 02 Hai Trieu Street, Saigon Ward, Ho Chi Minh City Role Attendee This was the kickoff of FCAJ Buildrathon 2026 (Season 01), a six-month contest of building real products for the Vietnamese AI and Cloud community. At the end, attendees had the chance to talk one-on-one with the HR team of CMC Global. The closing remarks recapped the key points, learning resources and upcoming community activities. Photos from the event Lessons learned and personal contribution A good bot starts with a solid architectural foundation. The speakers stressed designing the architecture before thinking about features. This matches what I am doing in Trust Check: separating request intake from processing with queues, so that each component can be controlled and scaled independently. I will apply this way of thinking from the start of future projects. Learn by doing. The hands-on session showed that prompt engineering, RAG, knowledge bases and AI agents become much easier to understand when tried by hand. I plan to spend time building a small agent on AWS to understand these concepts properly instead of only reading documentation. Read the task and the judging criteria carefully before starting. The organizers introduced the judging criteria and analyzed the task early, which showed me that understanding the requirements correctly matters as much as the implementation. From now on I will spend time clarifying goals and criteria before each project. Connect actively with the community. The networking session and the “Pay It Forward” spirit of AWS Study Group reminded me that teamwork and learning from one another are part of the profession. I will try to meet more new people and share what I learn. Prepare early for career direction. The chance to talk directly with the CMC Global HR team showed that companies value people who can build real products. I will polish my personal profile and present Trust Check clearly as a product deployed on AWS. This kickoff showed me that a technology contest is not only about writing code but also about how to think about architecture, how to work in a team and how to learn from the community. I carry this motivation into my next projects.

title: Blog 2
content:
🔐 UNDERSTANDING THE PHP2SHELL VULNERABILITIES: FROM EARLY DETECTION BY AMAZON TO MITIGATION WITH AWS WAF PHP2Shell is a critical security issue involving two vulnerabilities in PHP that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). What makes this incident particularly important is that Amazon Threat Intelligence observed exploitation attempts through its MadPot honeypot four days before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed.
This incident highlights how quickly attackers can exploit newly discovered vulnerabilities and why organizations must combine timely patching, continuous monitoring, and layered security controls.
Before examining the vulnerabilities, it is useful to understand several key terms:
Remote Code Execution (RCE): A vulnerability that allows an attacker to execute commands or code on a remote system. Honeypot: A security mechanism designed to attract and observe suspicious activity in a controlled environment. Embargo: A period during which vulnerability information is restricted from public disclosure to allow affected parties to prepare security updates. Proof of Concept (PoC): A demonstration showing that a vulnerability can potentially be exploited. Web Application Firewall (WAF): A security control that monitors and filters HTTP/HTTPS traffic to help protect web applications. Overview of PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and AWS WAF mitigation strategies. 1. Overview of the PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities affecting PHP’s handling of multipart/form-data requests:
Vulnerability Description CVE-2026-109618 Memory corruption associated with PHP running out of memory while processing a request. CVE-2026-109619 Stale data or global state from a previous request may be reused by a later request handled by the same worker. Both vulnerabilities can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution under affected conditions. They are rated Critical, with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.
The vulnerabilities are particularly concerning because the affected request-processing behavior occurs before the application code executes. Consequently, an application-level check may not be sufficient to prevent exploitation.
2. How Amazon Detected Exploitation Before Public Disclosure One of the most significant findings came from Amazon Threat Intelligence. Its MadPot honeypot infrastructure recorded suspicious activity before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed.
The following timeline summarizes the observations reported by AWS:
Date and time (UTC) Observed activity October 17, 2026 MadPot observed an exploitation attempt originating from a commercial anonymization network, four days before public disclosure. October 21, around 02:00 The first publicly available proof-of-concept material appeared. October 21, 02:00–08:00 Additional exploitation attempts were observed from anonymized infrastructure. Differences in payloads suggested the involvement of multiple actors. October 21, 14:00 The disclosure embargo was lifted and PHP security updates were released. After public disclosure Proof-of-concept material spread rapidly, increasing the likelihood of broader exploitation attempts. It is important to distinguish an observed exploitation attempt from a confirmed compromise. AWS stated that it was unclear how the early actor obtained the exploit information and whether the observed attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.
This finding demonstrates that defenders should not assume that a vulnerability is safe from exploitation simply because its public disclosure date has not yet arrived.
3. Why These Vulnerabilities Matter The PHP2Shell incident highlights several important security challenges.
3.1. Exploitation Can Begin Before Public Disclosure The October 17 observation shows that exploitation attempts may occur while vulnerability information is still under embargo. Organizations should therefore avoid relying exclusively on public disclosure dates when determining when suspicious activity may have started.
3.2. The Time Between Patching and Exploitation Is Shrinking Once technical details and proof-of-concept material become available, attackers can quickly adapt and develop their own exploitation attempts. AWS highlighted that AI-assisted analysis can further accelerate this process.
3.3. Critical Vulnerabilities Require Rapid Response For internet-facing systems, waiting several days to assess or apply a critical security update may create unnecessary exposure. Vulnerability response should be treated as an urgent operational activity, especially when exploitation attempts have already been observed.
4. Applying AWS WAF Mitigations AWS published guidance on using AWS WAF to apply additional mitigations for the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.
The managed rule group updates include:
Version 2.3: Introduced the PHP2Shell_BODY rule to help mitigate CVE-2026-109619. Version 2.4: Introduced the PHP2Shell_BODY_Extended rule to provide additional coverage for CVE-2026-109618. Version 2.4 became the default version on October 23, 2026. These rules provide an additional layer of protection, but they should not be considered a replacement for upgrading PHP.
4.1. Upgrade PHP to a Patched Version The primary remediation is to upgrade affected PHP installations to a fixed release.
AWS identifies the following patched versions:
PHP branch Fixed version PHP 8.5 8.5.12 PHP 8.4 8.4.27 PHP 8.3 8.3.36 PHP 8.2 8.2.35 For older PHP branches, organizations should review the applicable vendor guidance and available backported security fixes. Systems running end-of-life versions require particular attention.
4.2. Use AWS WAF Managed Rules Organizations can use the AWS Managed Rules rule group and its PHP2Shell-related protections to inspect incoming requests.
A cautious deployment approach is:
Enable the relevant managed rule group. Begin with Count mode to observe which requests would match. Review logs and investigate potential false positives. Move to Block mode after validating the impact on legitimate application traffic. This staged approach helps reduce the risk of disrupting normal application functionality.
4.3. Limit Request Body Size Request body size restrictions can reduce exposure to certain memory-exhaustion scenarios associated with CVE-2026-109618.
However, this is only a partial mitigation. AWS notes that request-header amplification and other factors can limit the effectiveness of a simple body-size restriction.
Therefore, body-size limits should be combined with PHP updates and appropriate server-side protections.
4.4. Restrict Unnecessary Multipart Uploads If an application does not require file uploads or multipart/form-data requests, administrators can consider blocking this content type through AWS WAF.
This reduces exposure to the affected request-processing path. However, it must be tested carefully because some applications legitimately depend on multipart uploads.
4.5. Apply Rate-Based Rules and Monitor Requests Rate-based rules can help reduce repeated suspicious POST requests. They are useful as an additional control, but they cannot guarantee protection against a single successful exploitation attempt.
Organizations should also enable AWS WAF logging and review suspicious POST requests, particularly those containing the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS parameter.
Important limitation: AWS WAF cannot fully inspect PHP worker memory or replace fixes to PHP’s internal request-processing behavior. WAF protections are defense-in-depth measures, not a complete solution.
5. Recommended Security Response Based on the AWS findings, organizations operating PHP-based applications should consider the following actions:
Patch affected systems: Upgrade to an applicable fixed PHP release as soon as possible. Review historical logs: Investigate suspicious activity starting from October 17, 2026, rather than only from the public disclosure date. Inspect suspicious POST requests: Look for unusual multipart/form-data requests and the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS parameter. Investigate unexpected activity: Review unexpected process execution and file modifications on affected servers. Evaluate suspicious IP addresses carefully: Commercial anonymization infrastructure may be shared by legitimate users. Investigate the associated activity instead of automatically treating every observed address as malicious. Deploy WAF protections: Use managed rules, logging, and appropriate request restrictions as additional defensive layers. 6. Lessons Learned The PHP2Shell incident provides several important lessons for security practitioners:
Embargo does not guarantee the absence of exploitation: Attackers may obtain or discover vulnerability information before public disclosure. Patch management must be responsive: Critical vulnerabilities affecting internet-facing services require rapid assessment and remediation. Monitoring must cover historical activity: Security investigations should consider the possibility that suspicious activity began before a vulnerability was publicly announced. Defense-in-depth remains essential: Patching, WAF rules, server-side protections, and continuous monitoring should work together. Security teams must adapt to faster exploitation cycles: Automated analysis and AI-assisted techniques can shorten the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation. 7. Personal Reflection and Conclusion What I find particularly important about PHP2Shell is not only the severity of the vulnerabilities, but also the timeline of the observed exploitation attempts.
The fact that Amazon MadPot detected suspicious activity four days before public disclosure demonstrates why security monitoring should be continuous rather than limited to responding after a vulnerability becomes widely known.
I also learned that AWS WAF can provide useful additional protection, but it cannot replace patching the underlying application. Security controls must be selected according to the actual limitations of the technology and the needs of the application.
For me, this incident reinforces an important principle in cybersecurity: effective defense requires early detection, timely remediation, and multiple layers of protection working together.
References Amazon Web Services. (2026, October 21). Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot.

title: Create the DynamoDB tables
content:
The system uses two DynamoDB tables: PhishingScanJobs stores each scan job and its result, and PhishingScanCache stores results for reuse during 24 hours.
Create the PhishingScanJobs table Open the AWS Console and select the Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Region. Open DynamoDB, choose Tables in the left menu, then choose Create table. Enter: Table name: PhishingScanJobs Partition key: job_id, type String Do not define a sort key. Under Table settings, choose Customize settings. Under Read/write capacity settings, choose Provisioned. For both Read capacity and Write capacity, set Auto scaling to Off and Provisioned capacity units to 5. Choose Create table. Wait until the table status is Active. Create the PhishingScanCache table Repeat the steps above with:
Table name: PhishingScanCache Partition key: target_hash, type String Capacity mode: Provisioned, Read 5, Write 5, Auto scaling Off 5 RCU and 5 WCU per table fit within the permanent DynamoDB free tier (25 RCU and 25 WCU in total), which suits the scale of this workshop.
Turn on TTL for both tables TTL lets DynamoDB delete expired items automatically. Both tables use the same attribute name, expires_at, which stores the expiry time as Unix time (seconds).
For each table in turn:
Choose the table name to open its detail page. Open the Additional settings tab. In the Time to Live (TTL) section, choose Turn on. Enter TTL attribute name: expires_at, then choose Turn on TTL. Table Value of expires_at PhishingScanJobs Job creation time plus 7 days PhishingScanCache Scan time plus 24 hours DynamoDB removes expired items in the background, which can happen later than the expiry time. For that reason the code always checks expires_at itself before using a cached result, and does not rely on the item having been deleted.
Result Both PhishingScanJobs and PhishingScanCache are Active in the Singapore Region. Both have TTL turned on for the expires_at attribute.

title: Error and cache testing
content:
This section checks how the system reacts to invalid input, a job that does not exist, a file that is never uploaded, and how the cache behaves. The commands use PowerShell. Replace <INVOKE_URL> with the address recorded in section 5.4.7.
Declare the address and a helper function that waits for a result, used in the parts below:
$base = "<INVOKE_URL>" function Wait-Scan($id) { do { Start-Sleep 5 $r = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan/$id" } while ($r.status -ne "COMPLETED") $r } Test 1: invalid input Send a request with an unsupported type:
try { Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan" -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body '{"type":"sms","payload":"abc"}' } catch { $_.Exception.Response.StatusCode.value__ $_.ErrorDetails.Message } Expected result: status code 400 and the body {"error":"invalid input"}. IngestLambda accepts only link, email or file as type.
Test 2: a job that does not exist try { Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan/khong-ton-tai" } catch { $_.Exception.Response.StatusCode.value__ $_.ErrorDetails.Message } Expected result: status code 404 and the body {"error":"Job ID not found!"}.
Test 3: an unsupported link The system analyses only http and https links. Submit a link that uses another protocol:
$job = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan" -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body '{"type":"link","payload":"ftp://example.com/file"}' $r = Wait-Scan $job.job_id $r.result.risk_level $r.result.details.error Expected result: risk_level is SCAN ERROR and details.error is ValueError: Chỉ hỗ trợ link http/https. An error during analysis is recorded in the result instead of breaking the system. In the web frontend this result is displayed as “Chưa kiểm tra được” (could not be checked).
Test 4: a file that is not uploaded Create a file job but do not upload anything to the upload_url:
$job = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$base/scan" -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body '{"type":"file","payload":"chua_tai_len.pdf"}' $r = Wait-Scan $job.job_id $r.result.risk_level $r.result.details.error FileDetectWorker waits up to 30 seconds for the file to appear in S3, so the command takes about 30 to 40 seconds to return a result.
Expected result: risk_level is SCAN ERROR and details.error is FileNotFoundError: Không nhận được tệp tải lên (hết thời gian chờ).
Test 5: the cache IngestLambda hashes the content of a link or email with SHA-256 and looks it up in the PhishingScanCache table before creating a new job. A result is written to the cache only when confidence is not LOW and risk_level is not SCAN ERROR. Results are kept for 24 hours.
The behaviour therefore depends on whether the API keys (section 5.4.6 or 5.4.8) are configured:
Situation What happens when the same link is scanned twice No API keys The result has LOW confidence and is not cached. The second scan creates a new job with a different job_id. API keys configured and the result is reliable enough The first scan stores the result in the cache. The second scan hits the cache. To check that the cache was written:
Scan a link (for example https://example.com) and wait for it to complete. Open DynamoDB, choose Tables, choose the PhishingScanCache table, then choose Explore table items. With API keys configured, the table has an item with target_hash, job_id, result and an expires_at equal to the scan time plus 24 hours. Without API keys, the table has no items. Known limitation in the cache branch. In the current version of the code, when the second scan hits the cache, IngestLambda can return an HTTP 500 error with the body Object of type Decimal is not JSON serializable. The cause is that DynamoDB returns numbers as Decimal, and the cache branch of ingest_lambda.py converts the result to JSON without handling this type. The branch that creates a new job is not affected.
To fix it, in the response function of ingest_lambda.py change the line 'body': json.dumps(body) to 'body': json.dumps(body, default=str), then Deploy the function again. The second scan then returns cached set to true, together with the job_id and result of the first scan.
Result Test Expected result Invalid input 400, invalid input Job does not exist 404, Job ID not found! Link that is not http/https SCAN ERROR with ValueError: Chỉ hỗ trợ link http/https File not uploaded SCAN ERROR with FileNotFoundError: ... after about 30 seconds Cache An item in PhishingScanCache when the result is reliable enough

title: Proposal
content:
AWS Phishing Detection Engine (Trust Check) This proposal presents the objectives, architecture, technical approach, implementation plan, and expected outcomes of the AWS Phishing Detection Engine (Trust Check).
1. Executive Summary The AWS Phishing Detection Engine (Trust Check) is a cloud-based cybersecurity platform designed to help users identify potential phishing threats through automated analysis of URLs, email content, and uploaded files.
The project addresses the growing difficulty of identifying sophisticated phishing attempts, particularly for users with limited cybersecurity knowledge. Rather than relying solely on a binary safe-or-unsafe result, Trust Check combines multiple detection techniques and external threat intelligence sources to provide an explainable Trust Score ranging from 0 to 100.
The platform adopts an event-driven serverless architecture built on Amazon Web Services (AWS). Its core services include Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS), Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3).
By separating request handling from asynchronous detection tasks, the system supports different scanning workloads, improves resource utilization, and reduces unnecessary processing through caching.
2. Problem Statement and Project Objectives 2.1. Problem Statement Phishing remains a significant cybersecurity threat. Attackers use fraudulent websites, deceptive emails, misleading URLs, and malicious file attachments to steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and distribute malware.
Identifying these threats can be challenging because phishing techniques continue to evolve. Traditional detection approaches that rely mainly on reputation databases or predefined rules may not identify newly emerging threats.
Furthermore, security tools do not always explain why particular content is considered suspicious. This can make it difficult for users without technical knowledge to understand detection results and make informed decisions.
These challenges highlight the need for an accessible and automated phishing detection platform that supports multiple content types, combines different analysis techniques, and provides understandable security assessments.
2.2. Project Objectives The primary objective is to develop a cloud-based platform that assists users in identifying potential phishing threats.
The specific objectives are:
Multi-Format Threat Detection: Support the analysis of suspicious URLs, email content, and uploaded files through specialized detection modules. Hybrid Detection Approach: Combine heuristic rules, content and metadata analysis, and external threat intelligence services. Explainable Risk Assessment: Generate a Trust Score from 0 to 100, accompanied by security classifications and explanations of detected indicators. Serverless Cloud Architecture: Use AWS managed services to support event-driven execution, asynchronous processing, and reduced infrastructure management. Efficient Resource Utilization: Apply caching mechanisms to minimize redundant scans and unnecessary external API requests. User-Friendly Interface: Provide a web-based platform for submitting content, monitoring scanning progress, and reviewing detection results. 3. Proposed Solution and Architecture 3.1. Solution Overview Trust Check provides three primary scanning functions:
URL Detection: Examines URL characteristics and domain-related indicators, with support from external reputation services such as VirusTotal, Google Safe Browsing, and URLhaus. Email Detection: Analyzes email content, embedded links, and relevant message characteristics to identify potential phishing indicators. File Detection: Performs static analysis of uploaded files, including file properties and threat intelligence checks, with MalwareBazaar as an additional intelligence source. After the analysis process, a centralized Scoring Engine evaluates the collected indicators and generates a Trust Score.
Trust Score Classification Interpretation 80–100 SAFE No significant threats identified by the available detection methods. 50–79 SUSPICIOUS Potential security risks detected; further verification is recommended. 0–49 DANGEROUS Significant threat indicators identified; users should avoid interacting with the content. The score is accompanied by explanations of the detected indicators. It represents an assessment based on the available analysis methods and should not be interpreted as an absolute guarantee that content is safe.
3.2. System Architecture The system adopts an event-driven serverless architecture with three primary processing layers:
Request Management Layer: Receives and validates user submissions through Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. Threat Detection Layer: Distributes scanning tasks through Amazon SQS to specialized workers for URL/email analysis and file analysis. Data Management Layer: Uses Amazon DynamoDB to store scanning jobs, detection results, and eligible cached information. Amazon S3 supports uploaded file storage and related analysis artifacts. The architecture separates URL and email processing from file processing. This allows workloads with different processing requirements to be handled independently.
Figure 2.1. High-Level Architecture of the AWS Phishing Detection Engine.
3.3. System Workflow The system follows an asynchronous scanning workflow consisting of the following stages:
Request Submission: Users submit a URL, email content, or file through the web interface. Request Validation: Amazon API Gateway forwards the request to the appropriate AWS Lambda function for validation and job initialization. Task Distribution: Amazon SQS distributes the scanning task to the appropriate processing queue. Threat Detection: Specialized workers analyze the submitted content and retrieve relevant threat intelligence when available. Trust Score Calculation: The Scoring Engine evaluates collected indicators and assigns a score and security classification. Result Storage: The completed result is stored in Amazon DynamoDB. Eligible results may also be cached for reuse. Result Retrieval: The frontend retrieves the job status and displays the completed analysis result to the user. For file analysis, Amazon S3 supports the upload workflow through temporary presigned URLs. This allows authorized uploads without exposing AWS credentials to the client.
4. Technical Implementation 4.1. Development Technologies The project uses the following technologies and services:
Category Technologies Frontend HTML, CSS, JavaScript Backend Python 3.12, AWS Lambda API Management Amazon API Gateway Asynchronous Processing Amazon SQS Database and Caching Amazon DynamoDB File Storage Amazon S3 Threat Intelligence VirusTotal, Google Safe Browsing, URLhaus, MalwareBazaar AWS Integration Boto3 Testing Python unittest Development Tools Visual Studio Code, AWS Management Console Version Control Git and GitHub 4.2. Detection and Risk Assessment The detection engine uses different analysis approaches according to the submitted content:
URL analysis examines suspicious URL characteristics and domain-related indicators. Email analysis focuses on message content, embedded links, and potentially deceptive characteristics. File analysis evaluates relevant file properties and static indicators of malicious activity. The collected indicators are passed to the Scoring Engine, which calculates the Trust Score and provides supporting explanations.
External threat intelligence services are used according to the content type and available integrations. Their availability, response limits, and service conditions may affect the completeness of the analysis.
4.3. Asynchronous Processing and Data Management Amazon SQS separates request submission from the actual detection process. This prevents longer scanning operations from unnecessarily blocking the initial API response.
Amazon DynamoDB maintains scanning job information and eligible cached results. Before starting a new scan, the application can check whether a valid previous result is available.
The caching mechanism helps reduce repeated analysis, unnecessary Lambda executions, and external threat intelligence requests. Cache expiration must be checked before a stored result is reused.
Amazon S3 supports file uploads and associated analysis artifacts.
5. Implementation Timeline and Milestones The project is carried out within the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) – Workforce Bootcamp 2026, from 14 September 2026 to 14 December 2026.
The following schedule provides an indicative allocation of project activities across the three-month participation period:
Period Main Activities 14 September – 13 October 2026 Define project requirements, identify detection objectives, design the system architecture, and prepare the AWS infrastructure. 14 October – 13 November 2026 Develop and integrate URL, email, and file detection modules; configure asynchronous processing, data storage, and threat intelligence integrations. 14 November – 14 December 2026 Complete frontend and backend integration, conduct functional testing, review detection results, document limitations, and evaluate AWS costs and optimization opportunities. The schedule is intended as a project planning framework. Actual task completion and evaluation results should be documented according to the implementation evidence.
6. Budget Estimation The project uses AWS managed services with consumption-based pricing models. Infrastructure costs depend on service configuration, resource consumption, deployment region, and actual scanning workload.
The project report presents a preliminary estimate of approximately USD 7.68 per month for a hypothetical workload of 10,000 scanning requests in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region.
This estimate is based on assumed service configurations and is presented before applicable Free Tier allowances and promotional credits. It should not be interpreted as a guaranteed monthly charge.
The main cost considerations include:
AWS Lambda invocations, memory allocation, and execution duration. Amazon API Gateway request volume. Amazon SQS message processing. Amazon DynamoDB capacity and storage. Amazon S3 storage and related requests. Amazon CloudWatch logging and monitoring. External threat intelligence service usage, where applicable. Actual costs should be reviewed using AWS Pricing Calculator and AWS Billing and Cost Management. AWS Cost Explorer can help examine service usage and spending trends.
7. Risk Assessment The project involves several technical and operational risks that should be considered during implementation and evaluation.
Risk Potential Impact Mitigation Approach Incomplete Threat Intelligence Detection results may lack relevant indicators. Combine multiple detection techniques and clearly communicate analysis limitations. External API Availability Third-party services may be unavailable or impose request limits. Handle integration failures and avoid treating unavailable intelligence as a clean result. False Positives and False Negatives Content may be incorrectly classified. Evaluate detection indicators, test different scenarios, and explain the basis of each score. Duplicate or Failed Tasks Scanning jobs may be processed more than once or fail during execution. Apply appropriate SQS retry settings, visibility timeouts, and Dead-Letter Queue policies where configured. Excessive Resource Consumption High workloads or repeated scans may increase AWS costs. Use caching, workload separation, resource monitoring, and appropriate configuration. Unauthorized File Access Uploaded files may be exposed if access is not properly controlled. Apply appropriate S3 permissions and use temporary presigned URLs for authorized uploads. Incomplete Scanning Results A failed or interrupted scan may produce an unreliable assessment. Track job status and distinguish incomplete or failed scans from completed security assessments. The Trust Score should be treated as a supporting security assessment rather than a guarantee of safety. Users should exercise caution when dealing with suspicious content.
8. Expected Outcomes The project aims to deliver a functional web-based phishing analysis platform with the following outcomes:
Multi-Format Detection: Support URL, email, and file analysis through specialized detection modules. Integrated Detection Techniques: Combine heuristic analysis, content and metadata inspection, and available external threat intelligence. Explainable Trust Score: Present a numerical score, security classification, and supporting detection indicators. Serverless AWS Architecture: Demonstrate the integration of API Gateway, Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB, and S3. Asynchronous Processing: Separate request handling from detection execution through queue-based processing. Resource Optimization: Reduce redundant scanning through caching and workload-specific resource allocation. Accessible User Interface: Allow users to submit suspicious content, monitor scanning progress, and understand the resulting security assessment. Overall, AWS Phishing Detection Engine (Trust Check) demonstrates how AWS cloud services can be applied to develop a modular, explainable, and resource-conscious cybersecurity solution for identifying potential phishing threats.

title: Event 3
content:
Summary Report: “Cloud Mastery” Event information Item Details Event name Cloud Mastery Organizer AWS Study Group Vietnam community (AWS First Cloud Journey AI) Speakers Khuong Huynh, Bao Nguyen, Phuong Huyen, Khang Duong Date Saturday morning, November 14, 2026 Location AWS Vietnam office, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Role Participant Cloud Mastery was a community session by AWS Study Group Vietnam on taking Agentic AI systems from prototype to production. Four speakers presented the core technical criteria, real-world case studies and deployment architecture on AWS.
Key takeaways From prototype to production. When bringing an Agentic AI system to AWS, three criteria must be met: security (Secure), reliability (Reliable) and scalability (Scalable). Cox Automotive case study. This was an Agentic AI use case at large enterprise scale, with more than 29,000 employees, 2.3 billion online interactions a year and 57 opportunities for AI. The focus was on building automation that users can trust. Duolingo case study. Their problem was that teams kept rebuilding the same infrastructure (“Every team rebuilds the same setup”). The solution was to standardize it into a shared platform, called the Shared Agent Platform. Scaling enterprise agents. When running hundreds of agents, thousands of tools, hundreds of MCP servers and more than 100,000 tool policies, Agentic AI infrastructure must be governed systematically. Security and identity with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. The framework has a standard 5-step architecture and two layers of authentication. Inbound Auth covers users accessing an agent through an application, using JWT or IAM through an Authorizer. Outbound Auth covers the agent accessing external resources. The system records the caller’s identity and issues a Workload Access Token (WAT). Deployment architecture on AWS. The sample model runs a Strands Agent on Amazon ECS, with the container image pulled from Amazon ECR, placed in the private subnets of a VPC, together with AWS Secrets Manager and other supporting services. Q&A and Quiz. The Q&A gave me more practical advice from the speakers on learning and Cloud and AI career direction. The closing Quiz helped reinforce what I had heard. Photos from the event Lessons learned and personal contribution Enterprise AI does not stop at an experimental model. I understand better that bringing AI into real use needs holistic architectural thinking, including shared infrastructure, identity security, governance of resources and policies at scale, and a secure network design on AWS. Share infrastructure instead of every team rebuilding it. Duolingo’s story showed me that standardizing on a common platform saves effort and keeps teams consistent. I will consider this approach when organizing projects with many components. Distinguish clearly who calls the agent and what the agent calls. The two-way Inbound and Outbound authentication model made me look again at how permissions work in Trust Check, where API keys are stored in Parameter Store and each Lambda has its own role with minimum permissions. I will keep applying this principle on larger systems. Build network design and secrets management into the architecture from the start. title: Architecture and data flow
content:
Architecture overview Trust Check is an event-driven serverless system. A scan request passes through API Gateway to an ingest Lambda, is placed on an SQS queue for workers to process asynchronously, and the result is stored in DynamoDB for the web frontend to query.
Components Component Role Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Exposes two routes: POST /scan to submit a request and GET /scan/{job_id} to fetch a result IngestLambda Validates input, checks the cache, creates a job and sends it to the matching queue StatusLambda Reads the status and result of a job from DynamoDB FastDetectWorker Analyses links and emails, taking work from the fast queue FileDetectWorker Analyses files uploaded to S3, taking work from the file queue Amazon SQS Three queues: fast, file and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) Amazon DynamoDB The PhishingScanJobs table stores jobs and results, the PhishingScanCache table stores reusable results Amazon S3 Receives user files uploaded through a presigned URL AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Stores API keys as SecureString parameters under the /phishing/ prefix AWS IAM Gives each Lambda the minimum permissions on exactly the resources it needs Amazon CloudWatch Stores the logs of the Lambda functions The Lambda functions use Python 3.12 on the arm64 architecture. The two workers can add results from VirusTotal, Google Safe Browsing and URLhaus to the internal analysis.
Data flow The web frontend sends POST /scan with a type of link, email or file, together with a payload. API Gateway forwards the request to IngestLambda. The function validates the input and returns a 400 error if it is invalid. For links and emails, the function hashes the content with SHA-256 and looks it up in the PhishingScanCache table. If a result that has not expired exists, the function returns it immediately. Otherwise the function creates a job in the PhishingScanJobs table with a pending status, then sends a message to a queue. Links and emails go to the fast queue. Files go to the file queue, and the response includes an upload_url so that the frontend can upload the file to S3. A worker receives the message, analyses the content, computes the trust score and writes the result into the job. For files, FileDetectWorker waits up to 30 seconds for the file to appear in S3. The frontend calls GET /scan/{job_id} at intervals. StatusLambda returns the status and, once the job is complete, the result. A message that fails processing several times is moved to the dead-letter queue so that it does not block the main queue.
Analysis result Each result has a trust score from 0 to 100 and a matching risk level:
Score Risk level 80 and above SAFE 50 to 79 SUSPICIOUS Below 50 DANGEROUS A result also has a confidence of HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW. When analysis fails, the risk level is SCAN ERROR. Results with LOW confidence and SCAN ERROR are not cached. The others are kept for 24 hours through the expires_at attribute used by DynamoDB TTL.
Why this architecture Asynchronous: the API answers immediately with a job_id, while the slow analysis runs in the workers, so one slow request does not block the others. Separated load: links, emails and files each have their own queue and worker, and each scales independently. Pay per use: every service is billed by usage, and no server runs continuously. Security: files go straight from the browser to S3 through a presigned URL, API keys live in Parameter Store instead of the source code, and each Lambda has only the permissions it needs.

title: Blog 3
content:
WHEN AI BECOMES A CYBERSECURITY “INVESTIGATOR”: EXPLORING AMAZON GUARDDUTY INVESTIGATION AGENT I used to think that when a security system detects suspicious activity and sends an alert, the next step is simply to check whether that alert is dangerous.
In reality, an alert is only the starting point. A Security Analyst may spend hours reviewing logs, correlating events, identifying affected resources, and determining whether an actual attack is taking place.
While reading the AWS Security Blog article about Amazon GuardDuty Investigation Agent, I came across an interesting approach: instead of having people analyze every alert manually, AWS uses an AI Agent to support the investigation process, gather evidence, and assess risk.
This post summarizes how the feature works. I hope it will be useful to anyone learning about Cloud Security and the application of AI in cybersecurity.
Amazon GuardDuty Investigation Agent 1. A FEW KEY CONCEPTS - Amazon GuardDuty: An AWS threat detection service that continuously monitors accounts and workloads to identify suspicious or potentially malicious activity. - Security Finding: A security alert generated when the system detects an anomaly. A finding does not necessarily mean that an attack has occurred. - AI Agent: An AI system capable of carrying out a sequence of tasks to achieve a goal. In this case, the Agent is used to collect, correlate, and analyze information for an investigation. - Threat Investigation: The process of investigating a threat to determine what happened, how severe it is, and which resources may be affected. - MITRE ATT&CK: A framework that describes tactics and techniques commonly used by attackers. It helps Security Analysts understand which stage of an attack suspicious behavior may belong to. 2. THE CHALLENGE: DETECTING AN ALERT DOES NOT MEAN UNDERSTANDING THE ATTACK Imagine that GuardDuty detects an IAM credential being used from an unusual location. This could indicate that the credential has been stolen. However, it could also simply mean that an employee is using a VPN or accessing the system from a new location.
To determine the cause, a Security Analyst needs to answer several questions:
Where was this credential usually used? Have any unusual API calls appeared? Has the account performed sensitive actions, such as changing IAM permissions or accessing important data? Are there other alerts related to the same account or resource? The challenge is that GuardDuty can detect suspicious indicators, but understanding the context and assessing the level of risk still require an investigation. As the number of alerts increases, manual analysis becomes time-consuming, especially for organizations managing many AWS accounts. 3. THE SOLUTION: AMAZON GUARDDUTY INVESTIGATION AGENT On July 20, 2026, AWS introduced Amazon GuardDuty Investigation Agent, an AI-powered feature designed to support the investigation of security findings in AWS environments.
Its key difference is that it does more than display alerts. It also helps analyze and correlate related evidence to produce a structured assessment report.
In simple terms:
GuardDuty: Detects that something suspicious may be happening. Investigation Agent: Helps determine whether those indicators are related, how serious the situation may be, and how it should be handled. According to AWS, this feature can reduce investigation time from hours to minutes. Investigation Agent is integrated directly into GuardDuty. Users can initiate an investigation through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, or SDK without having to build and operate a separate AI Agent themselves. 4. HOW DOES THE AI AGENT INVESTIGATE AN ALERT? According to AWS documentation, the process can be understood through four main stages. 4.1. Define the investigation scope Users can ask the AI Agent to investigate:
A specific GuardDuty Finding ID. An AWS account. All accounts in an AWS Organization that they are authorized to access. When using the AWS CLI or API, users can also provide a natural-language request through a trigger-prompt, with a maximum length of 2,048 characters. For example:
Investigate the recent unauthorized access finding. 4.2. Collect and correlate evidence After receiving the request, the Agent analyzes GuardDuty findings, correlates related activity, and considers the security context of the resources within the investigation scope.
Instead of treating each alert independently, it looks for relationships between indicators to build an overall assessment. 4.3. Assess the threat After the analysis, the Agent returns several important pieces of information:
Risk Level: The risk level, with the values Info, Low, Medium, High, and Critical. Confidence: The confidence level of the assessment, with the values Unknown, Low, Medium, and High. Summary: A summary of important findings and observations. MITRE ATT&CK Mapping: Links suspicious behavior to known attack techniques. Resource Mapping: Identifies the related AWS resources. 4.4. Recommend response actions The Agent does not stop at assessment. It also provides remediation actions prioritized by importance, which may include specific AWS CLI commands. This helps Security Analysts understand what they should investigate or address first. 5. AN IMPORTANT DISTINCTION: RISK LEVEL IS NOT CONFIDENCE This is one of the points I found particularly important when reading the documentation.
At first, I thought that if AI rated an alert as HIGH risk, it meant that it had confidently confirmed an attack.
However, Risk Level and Confidence are two different concepts:
Risk Level: Assesses how severe the threat is. Confidence: Indicates how reliable the conclusion is based on the evidence analyzed. Examples: Risk: Critical | Confidence: High → The indicators suggest a very serious threat, and the AI has a high level of confidence in its assessment. Risk: High | Confidence: Low → The threat could have a significant impact, but the available evidence is not yet strong enough to support a highly confident conclusion. My takeaway is that even a high-risk alert must be considered alongside the quality of the evidence, rather than judged only by a High or Critical label. A PRACTICAL EXAMPLE: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A SERVER IS COMPROMISED? In its article, AWS provides an example investigation result involving an Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) environment. The sample report shows:
A worker node with signs of compromise during operation. A reverse shell running with root privileges. Activity involving access to the Docker socket and execution of a malicious file. Approximately 500 runtime signals associated with multiple attack tactics. The Agent’s assessment was: Risk Level: Critical Confidence: High This example illustrates the value of analyzing multiple indicators together. If an administrator looks at only one alert, they may not fully understand the severity of the situation. By combining related indicators, however, the Agent can provide a more complete picture of the intrusion.
Note: This is a sample result presented by AWS in its documentation. It is not an attack that I personally performed or verified. 7. THREE STEPS TO TRY INVESTIGATION AGENT 7.1. Enable Amazon GuardDuty Open the AWS Management Console and make sure GuardDuty is enabled in a supported Region.
Then go to Investigations → Settings → Enable to turn on the investigation feature. 7.2. Initiate an investigation Under Investigations, select Initiate Investigation.
Depending on their permissions, users can enter a Finding ID, select an AWS account, or choose an organization-wide scope. 7.3. Review the assessment results After the investigation is complete, open the report to review:
An overview of the findings. Attack techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Risk level and confidence. Affected resources. Recommended remediation actions. According to the AWS article published during the Public Preview period, an account-level investigation typically took around 2–5 minutes, while an investigation of a specific finding took around 10–12 minutes. These are reference times from the preview period, not fixed guarantees for every investigation. 8. ANOTHER ADVANTAGE: INTEGRATION INTO A SECURITY WORKFLOW Investigation Agent does not have to be used manually through the AWS Console.
With APIs, organizations can integrate its investigation capabilities into their existing security monitoring workflows.
One illustrative architecture mentioned by AWS is:
GuardDuty → EventBridge → AWS Lambda → Investigation Agent → SIEM
The flow works as follows:
GuardDuty generates a security finding. EventBridge routes the event into the workflow. Lambda calls the API to initiate an investigation. Investigation Agent analyzes the information and returns its results. The results are forwarded to a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system for Security Analysts to monitor and handle. For example, findings assessed as Critical could be routed to a high-priority incident queue. The important point is that the AI Agent does not replace the entire security monitoring system. Instead, it adds analysis capabilities and helps prioritize alerts for further action. 9. CONSIDERATIONS WHEN USING THE FEATURE 9.1. AI does not guarantee a perfectly accurate conclusion Even when the Agent provides an assessment with High Confidence, the results should still be reviewed by a Security Analyst, especially before sensitive decisions such as locking an account or isolating a resource. 9.2. Apply appropriate IAM permissions To use the feature, AWS requires permissions such as:
guardduty:CreateInvestigation guardduty:GetInvestigation guardduty:ListInvestigations Not every account is allowed to initiate investigations across the entire organization. AWS has a separate permission model for administrator accounts and member accounts. 9.3. Pay attention to Region scope and data processing Investigation Agent uses a Cross-Region Inference mechanism to process assessments within the geographic scope specified by AWS. Data is stored in the Region where the request is initiated, but investigation data and summary results may be processed in another Region within the same geography.
Therefore, organizations with strict data-processing location requirements should review this aspect before deployment. 9.4. Check availability and cost At the time the blog was published (July 20, 2026), the feature was in Public Preview in 10 AWS Regions. It was available at no charge, with a limit of 10 investigations per account per day and a maximum of 100 investigations per account throughout the preview period.
These limits may change, so check the latest AWS documentation before trying the feature. 10. WHAT I LEARNED
Threat detection is only the first step. An alert becomes more useful when we understand its cause, related events, and potential impact. AI can help reduce repetitive investigation work. Instead of spending most of their time correlating alerts and compiling information, Security Analysts can focus on verifying results and deciding how to respond. Do not confuse severity with confidence. High risk does not mean that a conclusion is certainly correct. Both factors matter when assessing an incident. Automation does not eliminate the need for people. An AI Agent is a tool that supports the investigation process, but important security decisions still require appropriate human oversight and assessment. As someone learning about Cloud Security, I think Amazon GuardDuty Investigation Agent demonstrates a practical direction for applying AI in cybersecurity: not only detecting unusual activity, but also helping people understand what is actually happening and what they should prioritize. REFERENCES AWS Security Blog – Introducing the Amazon GuardDuty investigation agent: on-demand AI-powered threat assessment Amazon GuardDuty User Guide

title: Create the S3 buckets
content:
The system uses two S3 buckets:
Bucket Required Purpose phishing-raw-uploads-<ACCOUNT_ID> Yes Receives files that users upload directly from the browser through a presigned URL phishing-audit-logs-<ACCOUNT_ID> No Stores a JSON log of every scan at logs/<job_id>.json S3 bucket names must be globally unique. Replace <ACCOUNT_ID> with your 12-digit AWS account number. Use only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.
Create the upload bucket Open S3 in the AWS Console and choose Create bucket. Enter: Bucket type: General purpose Bucket name: phishing-raw-uploads-<ACCOUNT_ID> AWS Region: Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Object Ownership: ACLs disabled Block Public Access settings for this bucket: keep Block all public access selected Bucket Versioning: Disable Default encryption: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) Choose Create bucket. Configure CORS The browser uploads a file to S3 with a PUT request from an origin different from S3, so the bucket must allow that origin.
Open the new bucket and choose the Permissions tab. Scroll to Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) and choose Edit. Paste the following configuration and choose Save changes: [ { "AllowedHeaders": ["*"], "AllowedMethods": ["PUT"], "AllowedOrigins": ["http://localhost:8000"], "ExposeHeaders": [] } ] http://localhost:8000 is the address of the web frontend when it runs on a local machine (section 5.4.9). If the frontend is served from another address, add that address to AllowedOrigins.
Delete uploaded files automatically Uploaded files only need to exist while they are being analysed. A lifecycle rule removes them automatically.
In the bucket, open the Management tab and choose Create lifecycle rule. Enter: Lifecycle rule name: expire-uploads Choose a rule scope: Limit the scope of this rule using one or more filters Prefix: uploads/ Lifecycle rule actions: select Expire current versions of objects Days after object creation: 1 Acknowledge the S3 warning and choose Create rule. The code stores each file at the key uploads/<job_id>/<file name>, so the uploads/ prefix covers every uploaded file.
Create the log bucket (optional) This bucket is used only when the worker environment variable REPORTS_BUCKET is set. When it is not set, the system skips writing logs to S3.
Create the bucket phishing-audit-logs-<ACCOUNT_ID> with the same settings as above (Singapore Region, Block all public access, SSE-S3). This bucket needs no CORS.
Result The bucket phishing-raw-uploads-<ACCOUNT_ID> has Block all public access, CORS for PUT, and a rule that deletes objects with the uploads/ prefix after 1 day. If logging is wanted: the bucket phishing-audit-logs-<ACCOUNT_ID>. Note the bucket names, which sections 5.4.5 and 5.4.6 use.
